issues.title: Response shape is indistinguishable from a successful token response
issues.author: fkj
issues.body:
The deferred response defined in §4.3 reuses OAuth 2.1's response shape:

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L588-L648

Existing clients might read `access_token` from a token response and forward it as `Authorization: Bearer` to downstream resource servers.

### Options

We could consider moving the deferral token to a new top-level `deferral_token` field and imit `access_token` and `token_type` from the deferred response so naive clients fail closed.

Or we could say that since this is opt in, it's not a big deal. But in any case, I thought this was worth flagging to track.

comments.author: maxwellgerber
comments.body:
[Token Exchange](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8693#name-successful-response) had the same problem and decided explicitly to reuse the `access_token` field instead of omitting it:
> The access_token parameter from [Section 5.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749#section-5.1) of [[RFC6749](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6749)] is used here to carry the requested token, which allows this token exchange protocol to use the existing OAuth 2.0 request and response constructs defined for the token endpoint. The identifier access_token is used for historical reasons and the issued token need not be an OAuth access token.

> Or we could say that since this is opt in, it's not a big deal.

This is where I'm at - a client that opts in and then improperly handles the response is a broken client

comments.author: gniero
comments.body:
Failures might be tricky to track in some scenarios when using the token type - e.g. a client opts in to deferral (as an upgrade to  an implementation that already uses code flow), but its undelrlying abstraction (common on enterprise scenarios) injects an outdated library. 

Since authorization tokens should not be logged, it could take some time to track what is happening in the client side.

Aside from that, I like the token_type approach because it shapes the endpoint for multi-purpose token issuance.

issues.title: Originating-grant parameter set is not frozen at issuance
issues.author: fkj
issues.body:
The polling request only includes the `deferral_token` and the polling grant type:

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L669-L700

And the polling validation steps don't re-enforce any of the originating grant's parameters like scope, `redirect_uri` or any OIDC params:

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L702-L720

Two AS implementations can diverge on what is frozen vs. recomputed at resolution time. One could choose to e.g. snapshot `scope` at issuance, another re-evaluates current policy at the end and downscopes.

I think we should state explicitly that the AS MUST snapshot the parameters that influence the eventual access token (scope, `redirect_uri`, any OIDC params, etc.) and MUST issue the eventual access token under that snapshot.
But it might be that your use cases are different, so I'm interested in discussing if it would be useful to be more lenient.

comments.author: maxwellgerber
comments.body:
> AS MUST snapshot the parameters that influence the eventual access token (scope, redirect_uri, any OIDC params, etc.)

Agreed, though I don't know if this is something that can be written normatively or is better as an implementation consideration.

> MUST issue the eventual access token under that snapshot.

Not sure if I agree on this one. The AS should be able to incorporate the results of the long-lived task into the access token itself. For example, if not all scopes were approved, additional downscoping can occur during the deferral.

comments.author: fkj
comments.body: This would be a good discussion point for IETF I think.

issues.title: Error responses across endpoints are not aligned
issues.author: fkj
issues.body:
§4.5 distinguishes "already redeemed" vs. "unknown identifier" in `error_description`:

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L786-L793

§5.2 says that revocation "MUST cause subsequent polling requests against the deferral token to return `access_denied`" and that the AS returns `invalid_client` for cross-client revocation:

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L949-L998

This is an "exists for some other client" oracle observable by an authenticated attacker.

I think there might be some potential attacks here that we should consider. We already refer to RFC 7009 about indistinguishability, but I don't think the design here actually provides indistinguishability.

comments.author: maxwellgerber
comments.body:
It doesn't look like 7009 §2.2 references `invalid_client` at all - that is a hallucination 😓 

7009 states:
```
   The authorization server first validates the client credentials (in
   case of a confidential client) and then verifies whether the token
   was issued to the client making the revocation request.  If this
   validation fails, the request is refused and the client is informed
   of the error by the authorization server as described below.
```

However, the only error defined in 7009 is `unsupported_token_type`. For all others-

```
   The authorization server responds with HTTP status code 200 if the
   token has been revoked successfully or if the client submitted an
   invalid token.
```

So we should say
```
 2. If the deferral token is recognized but was issued to a different 
    authenticated client, the authorization server MUST return 
    HTTP 200 OK without modifying state, per {{Section 2.2 of RFC7009}}. 
```
instead.

comments.author: maxwellgerber
comments.body:
```
 - A `deferral_token` that is not recognized, was issued to a 
   different client, or has already been redeemed MUST result in an 
   `invalid_grant` error per {{Section 5.2 of OAUTH-2.1}}.
```

This link is wrong - should be [3.2.4](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1#section-3.2.4)

comments.author: fkj
comments.body:
> So we should say
> ```
>  2. If the deferral token is recognized but was issued to a different 
>     authenticated client, the authorization server MUST return 
>     HTTP 200 OK without modifying state, per {{Section 2.2 of RFC7009}}.
> ```
> instead.

I think this solves at least the main issue I was concerned about. But we should probably double check that there aren't any other attacks here.

issues.title: Missing guidance about OpenID Connect interaction
issues.author: fkj
issues.body:
For OIDC originating grants, ID Token claims can be captured at the originating authorize moment but the token is issued much later. This could cause trouble e.g. with `max_age` and `auth_time` in particular.

We should consider adding an "Interaction with OpenID Connect" appendix and consider whether we should:
1. State that ID Token claims reflect the originating authorization moment,
2. State that ID Token claims reflect the actual user authentication moment, or
3. Allow both options

comments.author: maxwellgerber
comments.body: This makes sense to me. I believe that `auth_time` should reflect the originating authorization moment. Since clients are opting in to the behavior of DTR, they should be equipped to handle the code changes necessary to deal with an older `auth_time` than typically expected.

comments.author: fkj
comments.body: I agree. The `originating authorization moment` could be a bit undefined in some cases, but maybe that's fine. E.g. in the case where there is an out-of-band interaction with the user while the flow is deferred, should the `auth_time` be the time of the original request/response or the time of the out-of-band interaction? I think the answer depends on the use case, but I think writing down some guidance makes sense.

comments.author: gniero
comments.body:
Since the spec allows both authentication or authorization to fit inside the deferral, providing guidance is the only thing that comes into mind. 

In my opinion, I'd use auth_time to specify when the user _authentication_ occurred tand not when user _interaction_ occurred. It is possible to request the authorization endpoint and the end-user may not be explicitly re-authenticated (maybe just a cookie gets validated). Honestly, I don't know if in such cases the auth_time gets updated in most deployments.

I wrote some use cases so we can discuss further:

Case 1: An user provides a password and a photo of its document. An immediate interim ID token would contain amr and/or acr according to the password (that is the only validated challenge so far) and its auth_time, and future requests to token endpoint could produce a new id_token with updated claims when the document gets verified.

Case 2: An user approves a payment transaction with passkey, but the authorization server relies on external verification tool. This process does not check for identity. If no identity is further validated, auth_time should be of the interaction time.

Case 3: An action initiated by an user by typing in a password must be approved by another individual. The client requests DTR and the AS reaches out the other individual (out of scope here) to request approval. The id_token should reflect the user interaction, not the time that second individual acted.

comments.author: fkj
comments.body:
> I wrote some use cases so we can discuss further:
> 
> Case 1: An user provides a password and a photo of its document. An immediate interim ID token would contain amr and/or acr according to the password (that is the only validated challenge so far) and its auth_time, and future requests to token endpoint could produce a new id_token with updated claims when the document gets verified.

I agree that this is the right way to do it in this case.

> Case 2: An user approves a payment transaction with passkey, but the authorization server relies on external verification tool. This process does not check for identity. If no identity is further validated, auth_time should be of the interaction time.

I agree.

> Case 3: An action initiated by an user by typing in a password must be approved by another individual. The client requests DTR and the AS reaches out the other individual (out of scope here) to request approval. The id_token should reflect the user interaction, not the time that second individual acted.

This one is kind of harder to manage, because it could be that the other person also had some user interaction. But probably the best thing to do is what you suggest. In general I think you would need something like the OIDC4AC idea that extends the `amr` claim if you care about the exact details here.

comments.author: fkj
comments.body: I don't think we need to solve this one before submitting the initial IETF draft. It could even be a separate spec as we've talked about.

issues.title: Discovery / opt-in in metadata
issues.author: fkj
issues.body:
The current discovery text suggests a non-supporting AS will silently ignore `deferrable=true`, but provides no normative MUST that a DTR-supporting AS publishes `deferred_token_response_supported=true` itself:

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L287-L294

I think we should say the AS MUST publish this.

The metadata also doesn't say which originating grants DTR is offered for, which we might want to consider doing.

comments.author: maxwellgerber
comments.body:
> I think we should say the AS MUST publish this.

Agreed, we should borrow the language used from [CIMD §5](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document-01.html#name-authorization-server-metada):

```
   Authorization servers that publish Authorization Server Metadata
   [RFC8414] MUST include the following property to signal support for
   client metadata documents as described in this specification.
```

> The metadata also doesn't say which originating grants DTR is offered for, which we might want to consider doing.

This one I am not so sure on - what would a client do with that information? How could its behavior meaningfully change? What if an AS impl changes over time and something that didn't support DTR now does?

comments.author: fkj
comments.body:
> This one I am not so sure on - what would a client do with that information? How could its behavior meaningfully change?

I think you're right that it couldn't really do much at this level. I can think of use cases where it would only be supported e.g. for some `acr_values`, but I don't think that's easy to negotiate in-band. That should probably be solved by providing client-specific metadata or something instead.

> What if an AS impl changes over time and something that didn't support DTR now does?

In that case they should "just" change their metadata, right? Or am I overlooking something?

issues.title: Mention that communication with any third-party approver/authenticator is out of scope
issues.author: fkj
issues.body:
AS could use some other provider/service/integration to actually do the authentication.
We should briefly mention the trust relationship there, but otherwise say anything about their protocol is out of scope.

issues.title: Retention guidance on "associated state" might be too weak
issues.author: fkj
issues.body:
§11.2 says the AS SHOULD dispose of `deferral_token` values "and their associated state" once the request has resolved or expired, but never defines what "associated state" is:

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L1283-L1293

I think we should at least mention the pieces of state that we mention elsewhere in the draft:
- the `client_notification_token`
- any snapshotted originating-grant parameters (see #2)
- any captured evidence

issues.title: Consider comparing with more specs
issues.author: fkj
issues.body:
The Relationship section contrasts only CIBA:

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L1057-L1085

Device Authorization Grant is contrasted inline in the beginning, but would make sense to do more in this section:
https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L133-L142

Might also make sense to compare to regular Token Exchange and First Party Apps.

issues.title: Explicitly mention  how to use `deferrable` with PAR and JAR
issues.author: fkj
issues.body:
The opt-in text says the client signals opt-in to DTR by including `deferrable=true` on the originating grant's token endpoint request.
I think we should add a one-paragraph subsection stating `deferrable` is conveyed wherever the originating grant's request parameters are conveyed (i.e. also inside the JAR request object or inside the PAR request body).

This might also require us to update the IANA usage location entry, but I don't really know to be honest.

comments.author: maxwellgerber
comments.body:
I like the language used in [9396 §3 ](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9396#section-3)[Authorization Request](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9396#name-authorization-request) - which ties the `authorization_details` parameter to existing usage of the `scope` parameter, and avoids needing to mention PAR and JAR as explicit vehicles. 

```
The authorization_details authorization request parameter can be used to specify authorization requirements in all places where the scope parameter is used for the same purpose, examples include:

authorization requests as specified in [[RFC6749](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6749)]
device authorization requests as specified in [[RFC8628](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8628)]
backchannel authentication requests as defined in [[OID-CIBA](https://openid.net/specs/openid-client-initiated-backchannel-authentication-core-1_0.html)]
```

Perhaps using related wording will make it easier to express opt-in semantics across different grant types as well?

comments.author: fkj
comments.body: Yeah I think it makes sense to try to rewrite with this in mind. That could also solve #26.

issues.title: Decide whether refresh token grants are included or not
issues.author: fkj
issues.body:
The "originating grant" definition lists Authorization Code, Client Credentials, and Token Exchange:

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L172-L179

But we do allow any originating grant as it is now. Refresh tokens have quite different semantics, so I think we should mention them specifically.
In particular, we need to think about how cancellation of a deferred flow affects the refresh token and whether a deferred response consumes the refresh token (probably not).

comments.author: maxwellgerber
comments.body:
> whether a deferred response consumes the refresh token (probably not)

For rotating refresh token implementations, I think a DTR _has_ to manipulate the refresh token in some way. Otherwise a single refresh token could be used to start multiple DTR polling flows, and we need some way to express whether each of those can result in the issuance of a new refresh token.

comments.author: fkj
comments.body: Good point. My mind immediately jumped to binding the refresh token to the polling flow, but I think the state management of that would be horrible. I think we need to discuss this in more detail and think through the interactions.

comments.author: max-stytch
comments.body:
Summing up a conversation from IETF 126 w @fkj @identitymonk @yaron-zehavi:

- We need to describe the expected behavior for OAuth 2.1 public clients using the refresh token grant type (which triggers token rotation semantics)
- We should make sure that whatever rules we apply to single-use refresh tokens are consistent with the rules for single-use authorization codes as well

Specifically, an AS needs to decide what to do with the original refresh token presented by the client when the AS decides to initiate a DTR flow. There are four mechanisms we can consider:
1. The refresh token is consumed at the beginning of the flow, and is exchanged for a deferred code 1-1. The deferred flow results in either success (resulting in a new refresh token) or fails (possibly freeing up the original token to be used again). As a result, a public client can only imitate one DTR flow per refresh token.
2. The refresh token is not consumed at the beginning of the flow, but at the completion of the flow. Multiple DTR flows can be started in parallel, but only the first one will succeed, triggering all the others to be cancelled.
3. DTR and the refresh token grant type are incompatible. You cannot use DTR with refresh tokens.
4. Sender constraining (such as DPoP) is **required** for using DTR with public clients, and as a result refresh tokens do not need to be rotated.

comments.author: yaron-zehavi
comments.body:
Thanks @max-stytch,
@fkj offered another option which I think offers benefits, which is refresh token is consumed when deferral is decided, and the client obtains in response a new refresh token which can be used for other flows (e.g token exchange) and a deferral code for completing the original token request.

issues.title: Enforce issues_token_type to match original grant
issues.author: fkj
issues.body:
We say that the successful polling response includes a `token_type`:
https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L722-L729

I think we should clarify that the `token_type` MUST match the originating one. E.g. for token exchange, this is important.
I suggest adding a line like:
>"When the originating grant defines `issued_token_type` in its successful token response, the successful polling response carries that originating-grant `issued_token_type` value".

issues.title: Specify that refresh tokens must also inherit DPoP binding
issues.author: fkj
issues.body:
§9.1 says the access token issued inherits DPoP binding to the same key:

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L1120-L1125

The §4.4.2 example response includes a `refresh_token`:

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L740-L753

RFC 9449 also normatively requires refresh-token binding for public clients.

We should add text along the lines of:
> For a public client (or any client that bound the deferral token with DPoP), the refresh token issued MUST be sender-constrained to the same key per RFC 9449.

issues.title: Polling-traffic side channels
issues.author: fkj
issues.body:
Polling patterns are visible to network intermediaries.
§11.1 mentions traffic observability in passing but provides very little guidance:

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L1270-L1280

I suggest adding:
- Clients SHOULD add upward-only jitter to their polling cadence to reduce fingerprintability.
- For AS-chosen `interval` values, be careful not to have different polling patterns for different flows/categories/etc. if that is sensitive.

issues.title: `error_description` progress string side channel
issues.author: fkj
issues.body:
§7 forbids PII in progress strings but the example value encodes the review category, which is then visible to anyone reading polling responses or downstream logs:

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L1036-L1054

We should add a privacy consideration that even the step name here might be sensitive depending on the process.
I think we should also change the example to be more opaque (e.g. just "in_review).

comments.author: gniero
comments.body:
Since the AS controls the authorization flow on a per-request basis, exposing its internal steps to the client could lead implementers to guess at the flow's progress, present inaccurate feedback, or even influence the user's decision. 

I think we could probably extend this feedback in interim id_tokens, under a profile.

issues.title: Interaction with introspection endpoint
issues.author: fkj
issues.body:
RFC 7662 only talks about access tokens. We should consider what an introspection endpoint should return for a deferral token (if anything).
Probably the AS SHOULD return `active=false` if a deferral token is submitted.

comments.author: maxwellgerber
comments.body: I don't think we need to make these tokens introspectable - all information an AS can convey about the token would already be returned through polling

comments.author: fkj
comments.body: I agree. I think we should call out the why explicitly though. Maybe just in considerations.

comments.author: gniero
comments.body: Since we renamed `deferral_token` to `deferral_code`, it's now clearer that introspection is not applicable

comments.author: fkj
comments.body: I agree with @gniero and will close this.

issues.title: Cancellation discovery before using
issues.author: fkj
issues.body:
A client could call the revoke endpoint against a non-aware AS. The client would then think the cancellation succeeded even though it didn't.
I think we should add guidance:
> Clients SHOULD check `revocation_endpoint_token_type_values_supported` before relying on cancellation.

issues.title: Potential polling loop with caching
issues.author: fkj
issues.body:
Polling success carries `no-store`, but polling-error responses don't require it.
If a polling-error response with `authorization_pending` is cached, the client might keep polling forever.
We should require `no-store` on polling-error responses.

issues.title: Normative references are tagged as informative
issues.author: fkj
issues.body:
The references block lists RFC 6750, RFC 8628, and RFC 8705 under `informative`:

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L46-L73

But RFC 6750 grounds a MUST for the callback Bearer header:

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L862-L867

And RFC 8628 grounds MUSTs for error code semantics:

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L763-L765

RFC 8705 grounds a MUST option in §9.1.

We should promote RFC 6750, RFC 8628, and RFC 8705 to normative references.

issues.title: Lowercase "should"
issues.author: fkj
issues.body:
A lowercase "should":

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L288-L294

The sentence describes behavior of a non-implementing AS, which this spec cannot bind normatively anyway. We should avoid using "should" and just say something like "will".

comments.author: maxwellgerber
comments.body: The lowercase should was removed in e6f6ac9336666c8a3d1737c8377160c89f80f233

issues.title: SHOULDs without motivation
issues.author: fkj
issues.body:
The `authorization_pending` SHOULD continue polling without any explanation for when it might choose not to:

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L767-L769

Clients SHOULD bind the deferral token with DPoP. We state the threat (long lifetimes) but not why it's allowed not to do it:

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L1109

`slow_down` SHOULD (I think this can be a MUST):

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L1147-L1150

SHOULD re-resolve (to avoid SSRF?):

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L1197-L1201

Clients SHOULD avoid embedding distinguishing information (also this is in a potentially non-normative section):

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L1279-L1280

SHOULD retain only necessary and dispose at resolution (also this is in a potentially non-normative section):

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L1287-L1290

comments.author: fkj
comments.body: We should consider this, but not a big deal before first draft.

issues.title: Pre-token hints confusing
issues.author: fkj
issues.body:
This is pretty confusing and tries to cover three things at once:

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L316-L323

As I see it, there are three options:
- AS didn't commit
- AS committed but can still satisfy synchronously
- AS committed and cannot satisfy synchronously

I think we should split this into more explicit text to avoid confusion about who should do what. Maybe we should list the cases more explicitly.

issues.title: Duplicate validation logic for `deferrable`
issues.author: fkj
issues.body:
The validation logic for `deferrable` is stated in the parameter definition:

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L267-L275

And then again in Pre-Token Request Validation:

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L466-L477

My feeling is that people don't really like normative language in definitions, so I think we should deduplicate so it's just in the validation logic.

issues.title: Duplicate "increase polling interval" rules
issues.author: fkj
issues.body:

issues.author: fkj
issues.body:
The current SHOULD-204 + MUST-accept-200 wording for callbacks is a bit weird:

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/487572d24861dcf388e00202bdadf4701fc28ea6/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L889-L891

comments.body:
This language comes from CIBA -

For valid requests, the Client Notification Endpoint SHOULD respond with an HTTP 204 No Content. The OP SHOULD also accept responses with HTTP 200 OK and any body in the response SHOULD be ignored.

issues.title: Unclear DPoP phrasing
issues.author: fkj
issues.body:
We write: "MUST present a DPoP proof on the initial token request that yields a deferred response":

issues.author: gniero
issues.body:
In §10.8 we say that `deferral_token` (now `deferral_code`) is a bearer-equivalent credential

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/e6f6ac9336666c8a3d1737c8377160c89f80f233/draft-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L1310-L1314

For the rest of the recommendation, no objection.

issues.title: Make the substrate contract for higher-layer profiles explicit
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Problem

DTR is positioned as a foundation that higher-layer profiles can build on, but the substrate's contract with those profiles is implicit. The guarantees an authorization server provides (e.g., that polling remains available, that the continuation handle is opaque, that authorization cannot be expanded after deferral) and the obligations a profile MUST preserve when extending the spec (e.g., state distinguishability, narrowing-only parameter updates) are scattered across §4, §5, and §9 rather than stated together.

Consequences:

- Profile authors re-derive the contract from scattered SHOULDs and MUSTs.
- Different profiles can interpret the same substrate behavior differently.
- Reviewers have no single anchor for evaluating profile drafts against the substrate.

## Solution shape

A single section that names the substrate's guarantees and the obligations on extending profiles, in one place. Constraints:

- Restates obligations already implied elsewhere; does not introduce new normative wire content.
- Doesn't change existing sections; pure addition.
- No new IANA actions, no new parameters.
- Located where readers encounter it before the wire-shape sections.

## Plan

PR to follow.

issues.title: Allow the preceding endpoint to return a deferred response directly, in addition to accepting an advance hint
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Problem

Today, when an authorization server defers a request for a grant that has a preceding endpoint, the preceding endpoint always returns its normal response (typically an authorization code), and the deferral decision is observed only at the token endpoint. `completion_mode=deferred` on the preceding request is a hint that influences the AS's later behavior but does not change the preceding endpoint's response shape.

This is correct for cases where the deferral is downstream of the preceding endpoint's normal operation. It is awkward for cases where the *authorization decision itself* is what is deferred:

- Front-channel step-up where the AS cannot decide whether to authorize until an out-of-band approval completes.
- Deferred ID Token issuance where claim verification follows the redirect.

In those cases, issuing an authorization code commits the AS to a decision it has not yet made. The code is later either redeemed against a deferred outcome (which works but is semantically odd) or unused (which leaks a credential).

## Solution shape

An OPTIONAL extension that lets the preceding endpoint return a deferred response directly, in place of the originating grant's normal response. Constraints:

- OPTIONAL. Authorization servers MUST be able to ignore the extension entirely and use the existing hint-only model. Discoverable via authorization server metadata.
- Does not change the default behavior of the preceding endpoint or the hint mechanism currently in §4.2.
- Preserves the substrate's invariants (continuation through the token endpoint, sender-constraining continuity, polling availability).
- Defines the wire shape only for the authorization endpoint in this iteration; other preceding endpoints (device, FIPA) can be addressed in follow-up profiles.
- Includes the PKCE handshake for public clients that need to defer at the authorization endpoint (verifier presented on the first polling request, not on subsequent ones).

## Plan

PR to follow.

comments.author: max-stytch
comments.body: Our rationale for always returning the deferred response from the `/token` endpoint is that it allows for DPoP binding. If we returned the deferral code directly from the `/authorize` endpoint, the client would not have an opportunity to present a DPoP proof - and since the deferral code is long lived by design this would be an issue.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body: DPoP can already be bound at the authorization request via the standard dpop_jkt parameter (RFC 9449). The AS binds the authorization code (or deferred transaction) to that JWK thumbprint, and the client proves possession when polling or redeeming with a DPoP proof. No new DPoP continuity mechanism is needed; just carry the existing dpop_jkt binding forward.

comments.author: max-stytch
comments.body: Oh, neat - I wasn't familiar with `dpop_jkt` but that sounds like it would do the trick. @fkj @gniero WDYT?

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body: I updated the PR to include language around this https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/pull/47

comments.author: fkj
comments.body: Yes I think we should definitely look into simplifying using `dpop_jkt`. Let's explore it!

comments.author: gniero
comments.body: I think it is a nice approach. We should probably add some considerations about `client_notification_token`. It should not be informed in clear at the authorization endpoint

comments.author: fkj
comments.body:
> I think it is a nice approach. We should probably add some considerations about `client_notification_token`. It should not be informed in clear at the authorization endpoint

Good point. I think we could require PAR to solve this?

issues.title: Add a polling-state vocabulary for "waiting on external interaction"
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Problem

The current draft has a single non-terminal pending state, `authorization_pending`, covering every case where a deferred request has not yet resolved. That includes both:

- Cases where the AS is waiting on automation (policy evaluation, attestation validation, risk analysis), and
- Cases where the AS is waiting on external interaction by a human (manager approval, document upload, step-up authentication).

A client receiving `authorization_pending` cannot tell which is happening and has no protocol-level way to surface an interaction URI to a user when one is needed. Profiles that need to convey "an actor outside the polling client must do something" either invent their own state vocabulary (fragmenting the substrate's state machine) or piggyback information into `error_description` (which is subject to data-minimization rules and not machine-readable).

OpenID Connect's `interaction_required` error code, registered in the OAuth Extensions Error Registry, already names this concept for the authorization endpoint. There is no token-endpoint analog today.

## Solution shape

A second non-terminal pending state in the polling state machine, distinguishable from `authorization_pending`, that signals "the deferred request is waiting on external interaction" and carries a URI identifying where the interaction can take place. Constraints:

- Reuses the existing `interaction_required` error name (already in the OAuth Extensions Error Registry); IANA action is a registration update to add token-endpoint usage.
- New response parameter (`interaction_uri`) registered in the OAuth Parameters Registry.
- Substrate-level vocabulary: the AS MAY transition between `authorization_pending` and `interaction_required` in either direction during a deferred request's lifetime; polling continues at the established `interval` in both.
- Client behavior is non-prescriptive: a client SHOULD present the `interaction_uri` to the user when appropriate but is not required to dereference or embed it.
- Does not change DTR's wire-shape or sender-constraining model.

## Plan

PR to follow.

issues.title: Discovery metadata review
issues.author: gniero
issues.body:
I've reviewed this in an earlier PR, but reading again, I had a second thought

https://github.com/maxwellgerber/deferred-token-response/blob/2c6e03dd0c13270ed7726800bf8fdbea861055a9/draft-gerber-oauth-deferred-token-response.md?plain=1#L317-L319

issues.title: Example deferral_code values conflict with the 128-bit entropy MUST
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
The deferred response section requires:

> The deferral code MUST contain at least 128 bits of entropy (160 bits RECOMMENDED) drawn from a cryptographically secure random source per Section 10.10 of RFC 6749.

Every example in the document uses `8d67dc78-7faa-4d41-aabd-67707b374255`, a UUIDv4. A v4 UUID carries at most 122 bits of randomness (6 bits are fixed by the version and variant fields), so the examples sit just below the MUST next to them. The format also invites implementers to reach for a UUID library, and not every UUID generator is CSPRNG-backed (v1 in particular is not random at all).

The value appears in five examples: the direct authorization endpoint deferred response, the deferred token response, the polling request, the callback notification, and the revocation request.

Two ways to resolve, depending on whether 128 was a deliberate threshold:

1. Keep the requirement and replace the example value with an unpadded base64url encoding of 32 CSPRNG bytes (43 characters), for example `V7e1gP8zT2mN4qR6sW9xY3aB5cD7fH0jK2pL4uQ6vX8`, optionally with a note that UUIDs do not satisfy the requirement; or
2. Change the entropy requirement so the examples comply, for example "at least 120 bits" with a note that a CSPRNG-generated UUIDv4 qualifies.

comments.author: gniero
comments.body:
This was probably inherited from the original OIDC draft we wrote in the past, where this value is also present. 
This one got by us over there.

Alternative *1* is aligned to quantitative requirements expressed by other attributes that have similar exposure (`request_uri`, `authorization_code`), so it seems a better solution to me.

comments.author: gniero
comments.body: I just checked CIBA examples and this happens over there. They have UUIDv4 for all the `auth_req_id`s and other attributes that require 128 bits of entropy in their examples

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body: The authors didn't have the privilege of having machines that read the specs and complain at you! Joke aside, it's a small nit that can get resolved before publishing.

issues.title: Deferral code revocation is not sender-constrained for public clients
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
Polling is sender-constrained: a public client's deferral is bound to a DPoP key, and every polling request must prove possession of it. Cancellation is not. The Cancellation section revokes a deferral code at the RFC 7009 revocation endpoint, where "the client authenticates to the revocation endpoint as required by its registered authentication method" — which, for a public client, is no authentication at all. The revocation semantics then act whenever "the deferral code is recognized and was issued to the authenticated client," a check a public client's client_id satisfies trivially since it is public information.

The result is an artifact that is sender-constrained for redemption but bearer for destruction. Anyone who observes a public client's deferral code — and the direct authorization endpoint deferral of #46 / PR 47 places it in front-channel URLs, browser history, and Referer headers under the default query response mode — can cancel the pending request. For deferrals backing long-running approval workflows, that is a denial of service that silently discards work a human may have spent days on, and the client discovers it only as `access_denied` on its next poll.

Suggested fix: when a deferral is bound to a DPoP key, a revocation request presenting its deferral code MUST include a DPoP proof with that key (RFC 9449 applies at any endpoint); a request without the proof is treated as presenting an unrecognized token per rule 2 of the revocation semantics. Confidential clients are already covered by client authentication.

Related: #42 discusses the bearer-equivalence framing in the security considerations; this issue is about the revocation endpoint's behavior specifically.

issues.title: Rehash use of deferral_code in Callback Notification
issues.author: maxwellgerber
issues.body:
From @bc-pi during IETF 126:
- AS must pass `deferral_code` to the Client a second time in the Callback Notification. Why? Sending the one-time secret over the wire twice is not great.

Raw Thoughts:
- This means the AS must store the `deferral_code` in plaintext vs storing a hash of the code after generation. Not great.
- Client currently uses `deferral_code` to identify the authorization transaction in a multi-tenant setup (where client has many users, and may be involved in multiple DTR flows at once), assuming the client isn't making use of `client_notification_token`, which could also be used to identify the transaction
- We could make `client_notification_token` required to get rid of `deferral_code` completely in the current setup, but that introduces new problems.
- Client generation of `client_notification_token` means that clients must generate a token (and potentially preemptively store state) on _every_ token request, even requests that do not end up deferred.
- @mcgiunnes 's proposal [here](https://mcguinness.github.io/draft-mcguinness-oauth-deferred-code/draft-mcguinness-oauth-deferred-code-processing.html) inverts the generation of the token and makes it the AS responsibility. This also has the benefit of playing with #46 #47 better since a `client_notification_token` wouldn't need to be passed to the AS at the `/authorize` endpoint

My first impression is to adopt Karl's proposal, move the notification token generation to the AS, and drop `deferral_code` in the notification response entirely. This moves us further away from CIBA, but that's probably fine.

issues.title: Is a new artifact worth the complexity? Why not just say it's a refresh token?
issues.author: will-bartlett
issues.body:
I was reviewing this spec subsequent to IETF 126. I was trying to understand how different a deferral code is from a refresh token. They both seem to be representations of the user session, which may or may not be able to successfully obtain access tokens.

The spec presents an example:

```
{
  "error": "authorization_pending",
  "deferral_code": "8d67dc78-7faa-4d41-aabd-67707b374255",
  "expires_in": 10800,
  "interval": 60
}
```

Couldn't the same example be written like:

```
{
  "error": "authorization_pending",
  "refresh_token": "8d67dc78-7faa-4d41-aabd-67707b374255",
  "refresh_token_expires_in": 10800,
  "interval": 60
}
```

The advantage of using a refresh token instead of a new artifact type is that there's no need to re-specify all the details about how session tokens should be stored, bound, etc.

It's already the case, under OAuth, that a refresh token may be valid for certain scopes and insufficient for other scopes, e.g. if certain scopes require MFA while others do not.

comments.author: gniero
comments.body:
Hi @will-bartlett,

The refresh token mechanism is bound to a grant that has already been issued, per [RFC 6749](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6749#section-1.5:~:text=as%20%5BRFC6750%5D.-,1.5,-.%20%20Refresh%20Token%0A%0A%20%20%20Refresh). It allows a client to remain accessing scopes / resources that were previously authorized, allowing the issuance of narrowed-down tokens. 

The `deferred_code` on the other hand represents an authorization request that hasn't completed yet.

Perhaps I didn't fully understand your proposal, but introducing new behavior to the refresh token would demand pretty much the same complexity for handling error responses, polling strategy, pre-token endpoint code issuance - and client logic to unambiguously handle tokens representing granted access from those that are still being processed.

If you have an idea how this could be solved in a simple manner, send us a PR and we will happily review it

We also have issue #10 to decide if deferral is applicable to refresh grants or not. This would potentially need a redaction

pulls.author: maxwellgerber

Remove the fallback language requiring servers to accept 200 OK, since clients are now required to respond with 204 No Content.

Closes #24

pulls.author: maxwellgerber
pulls.body: Fixes #23. The requirement to increase the polling interval by at least 5 seconds was duplicated in both the polling section and the slow_down error definition. Replace the duplicate normative text with a cross-reference to the canonical location.

pulls.title: editorial: replace normative "should" with descriptive "will typically"
pulls.author: maxwellgerber
pulls.body: The spec cannot bind authorization servers that don't implement it, so using "should" (an RFC 2119 keyword) to describe their behavior was inappropriate. Fixes #19.

comments.author: fkj
comments.body: Mentioned this in my review for #33 as well. Feel free to resolve that if this gets merged first.

pulls.author: maxwellgerber
pulls.body:
These three RFCs underpin MUST-level requirements in the spec and were incorrectly listed as informative. Also remove the `?` citation prefix from body references to RFC8705 and RFC8628, which marks them as informative in kramdown-rfc.

Fixes #18

pulls.title: Add client guidance for cancellation discovery
pulls.author: maxwellgerber
pulls.body:
Clients calling revocation on a non-aware AS receive HTTP 200 OK (RFC7009 §2.2), which is indistinguishable from success. Added a SHOULD requirement for clients to check
revocation_endpoint_token_type_values_supported before relying on cancellation to avoid silently failing to cancel a pending request.

Closes #16

pulls.title: Align error responses across polling and revocation endpoints
pulls.author: maxwellgerber
pulls.body:
Fixes #3. Two changes:

1. Revocation semantics: merge old clauses 2 and 3 so that a deferral token recognized but issued to a different client returns HTTP 200 OK rather than invalid_client. Returning invalid_client allowed an authenticated attacker to probe whether a deferral token exists for another client, violating RFC 7009's indistinguishability requirement. 

2. Token endpoint error responses: tighten the error_description SHOULD so the redeemed/unknown distinction is only surfaced when the server has confirmed the token belongs to the requesting client. Cross-client and unrecognized tokens MUST be treated as unknown with no distinguishing detail. Also update the cross-reference from Section 5.2 to the more precise Section 3.2.4 of OAUTH-2.1.

reviews.author: fkj
reviews.body: Generally fine, but see my one comment.

comments.body: RFC 7009 doesn't actually use the word indistinguishability, so we should probably specify more precisely what we mean here.

pulls.title: Replace 2xx response with 4xx error response
pulls.author: maxwellgerber
pulls.body:
Adopts feedback from email discussion to:
- Replaces the `200 + token_type + token` result with a `400 + deferred_token` error result.
- Introduce the `completion_mode` signaling parameter instead of `deferrable` parameter

A future PR (or... potentially future spec) can profile the error result to introduce the `interaction_uri` field from JAG-IR, transforming JAG-IR into a profile of DTR.

This touches on a number of open issues:
- #1: deferred response is now a 400 error with a top-level deferral_token and no access_token/token_type, so naive clients fail closed (resolved by the earlier response-shape redesign)
- #9: note that completion_mode is conveyed wherever the authorization request's parameters are, including the PAR body and a JAR request object
- #11: successful polling response carries the originating grant's issued_token_type when defined, and never the deferral-token type
- #17: require Cache-Control: no-store on every error response (including the deferred 400 and authorization_pending/slow_down) to prevent a cached pending response from causing indefinite polling
- #21: split the inconsistent-hint rule into three explicit cases
- #22: deduplicate the completion_mode validation rule, stating it once in the parameter definition and cross-referencing it from both validation sections
- #26: add a "preceding endpoint" definition to Conventions and Definitions

  Closes #1, #9, #11, #17, #21, #22, #26

reviews.author: fkj
reviews.body: A few nits, but generally looks good.

comments.body:
I think the examples in the middle of the definition makes it a little hard to read this sentence. How about something like (inspired by wording in https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6749#section-3):

```suggestion
: Some grant types utilize multiple authorization server endpoints. For an originating grant whose flow begins at an endpoint other than the token endpoint, the preceding endpoint is the endpoint utilized just before the token endpoint. Examples include the authorization endpoint of the Authorization Code Grant ({{OAUTH-2.1}}), the device authorization endpoint of {{RFC8628}}, and the authorization challenge endpoint of {{FIPA}}. A grant that operates entirely at the token endpoint (for example, the Client Credentials Grant) has no preceding endpoint.
```

This seems like a normative requirement:
```suggestion
SHOULD silently ignore the value and complete the request synchronously
```

Might even upgrade to a MUST, though it's hard to normatively require anything for non-implementers.

This reads a but confusingly: it's not a token response, but it still includes a token?
Maybe we should rename `deferral_token` to something else, or say that it is not an access token response?
Is this still relevant now that it is a new parameter instead of a token in the response on line 652?
Should probably reference RFC 7234 which defines the header.

reviews.author: mcguinness
reviews.body:
Strong convergence with my exploration

  - 400 + `authorization_pending` encoding. Same choice, same RFC 8628 alignment, same naive-client-safety rationale. The deferral token now lives outside the access_token slot, eliminating the credential-confusion risk.
  - `completion_mode` request parameter with deferred as initial value. Same parameter name, OAuth Completion Mode Values registry, & Specification Required policy.
  - Cache-Control: no-store on all error responses including pending/slow_down. Preserves the substrate's response-handling rules.
  - Successful polling response carries the originating grant's `issued_token_type` and never `urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:deferral-token`. Same conclusion; the deferral artifact is segregated to the deferred response.
  - `authorization_pending` reused for both initial deferred response and subsequent polling responses. Same dual-role choice, with the rotation/repeat rules folded in correctly.

comments.body: I preferred `deferred_code` in my exploration to address a similar concern and align better with device_code/auth_req_id precedent (RFC 8628, CIBA)

This is a clean recipe but has limits:

  - It assumes the immediate result and the deferred result are independent. For interim ID Tokens (where the interim and complete representations are semantically tied — same claim set, one populated now, one populated later), the parallel-grant approach can't model the relationship.
  - It requires the client to initiate two grants. For high-frequency calls this is more wire overhead than a single response with both artifacts.

My substrate exploration took an alternate approach: a partial completion response (200 OK with both an issued artifact AND a deferred_code for upgrade) carries both in one request:

  POST /token grant_type=authorization_code&code=...&completion_mode=deferred grant_mode=interim
  → 200 OK with id_token (interim claims) + deferred_code + deferred_code_expires_in

Continuation polling returns the upgraded artifact. The partial completion wire shape is substrate-level; the interim semantics (replacement on upgrade) live in a companion spec (my example was draft-mcguinness-oauth-interim-grant-mode)

The PR keeps a hint-only model: `completion_mode=deferred`on the preceding endpoint is an advance hint, but the deferred response itself only comes from the token endpoint. My substrate exploration supports direct deferral at the authorization endpoint, the redirect carries a `deferred_code` instead of code, so no authorization code is ever issued for flows that won't complete synchronously.

Concretely, the substrate exploration covers a flow like:

```
GET /authorize?...&completion_mode=deferred  → 302 with deferred_code in redirect (no code)
POST /token grant_type=urn:...:deferred_code&deferred_code=...&code_verifier=...
```

DTR's flow always issues a code first:

```
GET /authorize?...&completion_mode=deferred  → 302 with code
POST /token grant_type=authorization_code&code=...&completion_mode=deferred  → 400 deferral_token
```

The difference matters for cases where the authorization decision itself is what's deferred (front-channel step-up, deferred ID Token issuance). The hint-only model still issues an authorization code while the underlying decision is pending, which is awkward for those cases.

If interim ID Tokens or front-channel step-up are in scope, direct authorization-endpoint deferral needs to be considered. If they're out of scope, DTR's hint-only model is simpler and adequate.

reviews.author: gniero
reviews.body: Hello @maxwellgerber, I've added some observations as well

comments.body:
This paragraph seems to narrow down the behavior of "silently ignore" only in cases where `completion_mode` is `deferred`. 

Is our intention to instruct implementers on  behavior of the `deferral` value, or for all of the `completion_mode` values that may be available in the future?

I have use cases that are front-channel step-up, and I understand you point of view. The authorization code serves as a transport rather represents the outcome of the authorization request, and this behavior may require additional implementation to provide proper user feedback and application flow control

Being this is not a pairwise combination, I'm afraid we could be contributing  on a scenario where intermitent errors might occur - and they may be tricky to track. In many implementations, the application requesting the token endpoint is not the same as the one requesting authorization.

If this is a behavior we want to keep, we could probably add an implementation consideration

> It assumes the immediate result and the deferred result are independent.

Yes, that's the main gap. I think this gap will be more apparent when it comes to access tokens, especially if implementers try to encode some semblance of RAR payloads where the content changes often. I'm not as worried about the semantic ties of ID Tokens - because ID Token claims tend to be fairly static and `?prompt=none` has always existed.

I think this will be something we explicitly look for feedback on from the wider community. If there is a clear demand to support the intermediate+deferred result we should revisit the model from your draft. The chief problem with a 200 response is that it creates an explosion of options:
- If DTR isn't needed, return 200 + tokens
- If DTR is needed but we can return an intermediate result, return 200 + intermediate tokens + deferred code
- If DTR is needed and we cannot return a result, return 400 + deferred code 

Add in a JAG-IR profile where the deferred code can _also_ include a URL for user interaction and we have a lot of complexity. 

I wonder if we can leave the door open in such a way that this RFC defines the 400 case, and a _future_ RFC could define intermediate results + deferred code in the 200 case, if the ecosystem wants it?

> If interim ID Tokens or front-channel step-up are in scope, direct authorization-endpoint deferral needs to be considered. If they're out of scope, DTR's hint-only model is simpler and adequate.

Responded above - I wonder if we can leave the door open on this draft s.t. a future draft can define interim results - like interim ID tokens on top.

> The difference matters for cases where the authorization decision itself is what's deferred (front-channel step-up, deferred ID Token issuance). The hint-only model still issues an authorization code while the underlying decision is pending, which is awkward for those cases.

If we issue a `deferred_code` directly from the /authorize endpoint and not from the /token endpoint, then we special-case the authorization code flow in a way that puts us at odds with using DTR for other grant types that only deal with the /token endpoint. Not insurmountable, but I would prefer to keep all grants the same if possible.
Good catch - since we are defining the `completion_mode ` parameter we should define the default behavior for all cases where the AS does not support it.
What if we tightened the behavior of the AS, such that it always rejected the error with `invalid_request`?

I like `deferral_code` - `deferred_` implies that it is a regular code that has been deferred, while `deferral_` indicates the `code` identifies the deferral instance itself, which I think is closer to what we want to represent.

I'll do a rename in a separate PR - it is a rather substantial edit.
Let's get rid of this para

I agree @maxwellgerber, it's not a 100% clear that the interim ID token is really necessary. We originally introduced the concept more because we easily could than because we have a must-have use case. In every case it's more of a nice-to-have that lets relying parties do some work up-front if they are pretty confident that the final verdict will be good (this would of course need to be measured for each use case).
I would support leaving it as an extension point if we can find a way to do that.

pulls.title: Add Substrate Invariants section
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Resolves #44.

Adds a new `# Substrate Invariants` section positioned after `# Overview` and before `# Client Opt-In Signaling`. The section has two subsections:

- **Substrate Guarantees** — six invariants the authorization server provides (no authorization expansion; continuation through the token endpoint; sender-constraining continuity; originating request immutability through the polling grant type; opaque continuation reference; polling is always available as an authoritative completion path).
- **Profile Obligations** — three obligations any extending profile MUST satisfy (state distinguishability, narrowing-only parameter updates, no relaxation of guarantees).

Per the issue, the section restates obligations already implied by §4, §5, and §9 rather than introducing new normative wire content. No existing text is modified. No new IANA actions or parameters.

### Files changed

- `draft-gerber-oauth-deferred-token-response.md`: +71 lines, new section after Overview.

### Source

Section adapted from `§Substrate Invariants` in `draft-mcguinness-oauth-deferred-code-processing`.

pulls.title: Add optional direct deferral at the authorization endpoint
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Resolves #46.

Adds a new `## Direct Preceding-Endpoint Deferral` subsection under `# The Deferred Authorization Grant`, immediately after `## Pre-Token Response`. The section defines an OPTIONAL extension in which the authorization endpoint returns a deferred response directly (a redirect carrying `deferral_code`) in place of the originating grant's normal response.

The default behavior (hint-only at the preceding endpoint) is unchanged. Authorization servers that do not support direct deferral can ignore the extension entirely.

### What the section defines

- **When direct deferral applies**: only when the authorization server signals support via the new `deferred_authorization_endpoint_supported` metadata flag.
- **Wire shape for the authorization endpoint**: the redirect carries `deferral_code`, `state`, `expires_in`, and optionally `interval`, in place of the normal `code` parameter. Uses the same `response_mode` (`query` or `form_post`) the authorization request selected. `response_mode=fragment` SHOULD NOT be used; rationale included.
- **Sender-constraining requirements**: the `deferral_code` is not single-use (unlike an authorization code), so sender-constraining is required both at the authorization response and on every polling request. PKCE is REQUIRED on the authorization request for all clients (extending RFC 9700 §2.1.1 to confidential clients). Every polling request MUST be sender-constrained by client authentication or by DPoP bound via `dpop_jkt` (RFC 9449). Public clients MUST use `dpop_jkt`.
- **PKCE-on-first-polling mechanics**: `code_verifier` is presented on the first polling request (as an exception to the polling-request prohibition on parameters that modify the originating request) and MUST NOT be re-presented on subsequent polling requests.
- **DPoP binding mechanics**: `dpop_jkt` on the authorization request binds the JWK thumbprint to the deferral state; the AS verifies DPoP proofs on every polling request against the bound thumbprint. Addresses the sender-constrained credential concern raised on the issue.
- **Other preceding endpoints**: out of scope for this iteration; a future profile can extend the wire shape to the device authorization endpoint of RFC 8628 or the authorization challenge endpoint of FIPA.

### Security Considerations

Adds `## Direct Preceding-Endpoint Deferral` to Security Considerations. The `deferral_code` is delivered via the authorization response and is thus exposed to browser history, referrer headers, and redirection-target access logs — the same vectors RFC 9700 identifies for authorization codes. Combined with the deferral code's long lifetime and multi-use presentation on polling, an unbound `deferral_code` has an impact comparable to an intercepted refresh token. This motivates the stricter sender-constraint requirements above.

### IANA addition

- `deferred_authorization_endpoint_supported`: Boolean AS metadata. Default `false`. When `true`, the AS supports direct deferral at the authorization endpoint.

### Files changed

- `draft-gerber-oauth-deferred-token-response.md`: +172 lines, new subsections plus IANA registration entry and security consideration.

### Source

Adapted from `§Authorization Endpoint Extensions` in `draft-mcguinness-oauth-deferred-code-processing`. The metadata parameter name `deferred_authorization_endpoint_supported` is shortened from the source draft's verbose name and is endpoint-specific (the section anchor `direct-preceding-endpoint-deferral` is general for forward extensibility).

pulls.title: Add interaction_required token-endpoint state and interaction_uri response parameter
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Resolves #48.

Adds a second non-terminal pending state to the polling state machine, distinguishable from `authorization_pending`, for cases where the deferred request is waiting on external interaction. Pairs the new state with an `interaction_uri` response parameter that identifies where the interaction can take place.

### What the PR adds

- **New `interaction_required` error code in §5.6 (Token Endpoint — Error Responses)**, alongside the existing `authorization_pending`, with clarifying text that:
  - `authorization_pending` is for pending requests *not* waiting on external interaction.
  - `interaction_required` is for pending requests waiting on external interaction; the response MUST include `interaction_uri`.
  - Both are non-terminal; the AS MAY transition between them in either direction.
  - Polling continues at the established `interval` in both states.
- **New `interaction_uri` response parameter** documented in §5.4 (Token Endpoint — Deferred Response), defined as OPTIONAL on `authorization_pending` responses and REQUIRED on `interaction_required` responses. The URI MUST be HTTPS, MUST NOT contain a fragment, and is bound to the deferral state.
- **Example** showing an `interaction_required` response with `interaction_uri`.
- **Cross-reference to §interaction-required-error** wherever needed.

### IANA actions

- **Register `interaction_uri`** in the OAuth Parameters Registry (token response location).
- **Update the existing `interaction_required` registration** in the OAuth Extensions Error Registry (originally registered by OpenID Connect Core for authorization endpoint use) to add token endpoint response usage. Change controller note credits OIDF for the original authorization-endpoint registration and IETF for the token-endpoint addition.
- Add OIDC-CORE to informative references (used by the registry-update note).

### Why reuse `interaction_required` rather than minting a new error name

OpenID Connect already registered the name for the same conceptual condition (external interaction is required). Reusing it preserves cross-spec vocabulary alignment and avoids cluttering the registry. The IANA registration update is the established mechanism for adding response locations to existing error codes.

### Files changed

- `draft-gerber-oauth-deferred-token-response.md`: +95/-7 lines. New error code, new parameter, new example, IANA registration update, informative reference addition.

### Source

Adapted from `§Deferred Error Semantics` and `§Interaction URI Parameter` in `draft-mcguinness-oauth-deferred-code-processing`.
